q: Why does a slightly wrong camera LUT shift skin?
a: A LUT made for another log curve (F-Log vs F-Log2) looks almost right but shifts skin, because it expects different input values. In Revolution, let colour management do the transform: set the clip to Fujifilm F-Log2 / F-Gamut if it isn't detected and the sequence to DaVinci Wide Gamut / Intermediate; don't add a camera LUT on top, or the transform happens twice.

q: Why label the first node Balance?
a: The first node fixes exposure and white balance (Offset / Gain, Temperature / Tint or the WB picker) so a look can sit on a neutral picture; labelling it Balance (`grade.labelNode`) keeps the tree readable. But neutral isn't always right: a sunset or tungsten scene should stay warm, so balance to what the scene should feel like.

q: Why use the waveform instead of my eyes for blacks and whites?
a: Monitors and eyes adapt; the waveform doesn't. Bring the lowest trace near the bottom with Lift and the highest near the top with Gain on the balance node; `scopes.read` gives the numbers. Not every shot should reach both ends (fog, night, a soft look).

q: Where should I set the pivot before adding contrast?
a: Set Pivot to the brightness of the subject's face, then add Contrast: contrast always pivots somewhere, and choosing the point keeps faces stable. Strong contrast also raises saturation, so check skin afterwards.

Contrast changes how saturated colours look, so setting saturation first means doing it twice. Raise Saturation on the node after contrast and watch the vectorscope; skin goes orange quickly, and strong reds and blues can clip on a Rec. 709 delivery.

q: How do I read one face on the vectorscope in a busy shot?
a: Isolate the face with a window on a node to read it alone, then see whether its trace lies along the skin-tone line. All skin falls near one hue direction whatever its depth; the line is a guide, not a target.

q: Why do skin mattes chatter on movement?
a: Hard mattes flicker as the face moves through the selection's edges. Raise Qualifier softness (and Matte blur if speckled), keep the selection a little wider, and limit wood or walls that share skin's hue with a window.

q: Why add a window to a sky qualifier?
a: The window keeps blue clothes and reflections out, while the qualifier follows the horizon's shape; together on one node the change lands only on the sky. A blown white sky has no colour to qualify; a gradient alone or a replacement is the only fix.

Eyes go to the brightest area first, so slightly darker, very soft edges move attention to the subject without the viewer noticing. In Revolution: an inverted, very soft ellipse window on its own node with Gain down a little, tracked if the subject moves.

q: Why keep corrections and the look on separate nodes?
a: Corrections differ per shot; the look shouldn't. A late look node (curves, wheels or a LUT with its mix) can be copied to other shots with Append Grade and dialled up or down. Revolution has no shared or group nodes yet, so re-append the look node after changing it.

A colour mismatch is often a level mismatch in one channel, so match black level, then white level, then midtones, then colour and saturation. In Revolution: a still of the reference, wipe, Shot Match for a first pass, then fine-tune and check with Compare shots.

q: Why cool and desaturate for day for night?
a: At night eyes see less colour and a bluer world, and light comes from sources rather than the sky. So bring exposure down a lot, cool the picture, lower saturation, darken the sky most and keep lights and eyes brighter with windows.
